confidence_why: Van Gysel's 2024 dissertation measures greatest prominence on the final syllable of most Sanapaná nouns in isolation and Silva Gomes's 2013 dissertation independently calls final stress the language's default, so the two fieldworkers agree on placement and the only caveats are details: an extra prominent syllable two before the end, token-to-token variation and a few non-final forms noted by Van Gysel (2017, 2024) and Silva Gomes (2013).

Of 47 investigated tokens in isolation (and thus presumably in their citation form), the second syllable has higher pitch at the midpoint of the vowel than the first in 40 cases. ... new_statements.quote: [fn. 2, p. 27] If the tress in Spanish loans is maintained and results therefore in an abnormal position for Sanapaná (i.e. preceding the last syllable), this is indicated by means of an acute accent on the stressed syllable. In this case, stress is adapted to the Sanapaná system (vak’ka). [p. xii] ’ stress lies on the next syllable [pp. 47-48] they always encliticise to the preceding word, forming together one phonetic unit. In this process, stress shifts away from the root and onto the clitic: as such, forms such as enenta:men’aɬta (from enen’ta:men ‘past’), keɬwoje’ɬke (from keɬwo’je ‘moment’) and pesa:sepha’ta (from pe’sa:sep) are created.

new_statements.relation_note: Placement agrees with the catalog's fixed: final syllable rule (final stress): the only explicit statement treats non-final stress as abnormal and nativises a loan with final stress. The work adds detail the catalog lacks: the stress domain includes enclitic particles (stress shifts to the end of the host+clitic unit), Spanish loans can retain non-final stress, and some cited forms with long vowels show stress on the long penult. No existing_statements were on record for this language, so this is the first quoted statement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress normally falls on the last syllable: stress 'preceding the last syllable' is called 'an abnormal position for Sanapaná', and the Spanish loan vaca is nativised as vak’ka with final stress (the mark ’ precedes the stressed syllable). Temporal particles (aɬta, ɬke, hata) are enclitics that form one phonological word with their host, and stress moves off the root to the end of the clitic group (keɬwoje’ɬke, pesa:sepha’ta).
new_statements.exceptions: Spanish loans may keep their original non-final stress, written with an acute (e.g. mésa 'table' in ex. 26a, p. 31). The author's own base forms enen’ta:men 'past' and pe’sa:sep 'night' carry the stress mark on a long penultimate vowel rather than the final syllable, and enenta:men’aɬta places it on the first syllable of the two-syllable clitic; the author does not comment on this, but it suggests that long vowels attract stress (a weight effect) or that the stress mark is placed loosely. No statement on tone; the work states it did not focus on phonology.
new_statements.identity_note: Van Gysel's Sanapaná data come from his own 2016-2017 fieldwork in the community of La Esperanza (Paraguayan Chaco); the thesis also compares Angaité, Enxet, Enlhet, Guaná and Enenlhet, but the stress statements quoted are about Sanapaná itself. He notes that the phonology sketch leans on Gomes (2013) and Kalisch (2009) and that he did not focus on phonology.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between the one listed work and the catalog: Van Gysel (2017) treats stress before the last syllable as 'an abnormal position for Sanapaná' and nativises loans with final stress, matching the catalog's final-stress rule. One internal wrinkle: his own transcriptions enen’ta:men and pe’sa:sep mark stress on a long penultimate vowel, and enenta:men’aɬta marks it on the first syllable of the clitic aɬta, so the thesis's examples are not uniformly final; he never discusses this, so it is at most a hint of weight sensitivity (long vowels attracting stress), not a stated rule. 33), while noting a form je’phophea with non-final stress

audit.reasoning: Quote check: the deciding passage is verbatim in the held Van Gysel 2024 PDF/txt at the stated pages (151, 153-157). Deciding source is the best available: a 2024 dissertation-grammar by the language's main documenter with Praat measurements; no later or more specialised prosody study exists in Glottolog or Crossref. The one competing grammar-length work (Silva Gomes 2013, UNICAMP) was downloaded from the open UNICAMP repository and read: it has no stress section but states (fn.32 p.96; pp.128-129) that stress falls preferentially on the word-final syllable, is the Sanapaná default, and is 'defined locally, not by syllable type' — independently confirming our right-edge/final coding and the no-weight note.
